Large optimization models are often made of independent blocks that interact only
through a few **linking variables** or a few **linking constraints**. Decomposition
methods exploit exactly this. Benders decomposition [@benders1962] fixes the linking
variables and lets the blocks answer with cuts. Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition
[@dantzig1960] prices the linking constraints and lets the blocks answer with columns.

```{python}
#| label: fig-structures
#| fig-cap: "The two block structures. Left: linking variables (an orange column), exploited by Benders decomposition. Right: linking constraints (an orange row), exploited by Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition. Blue: independent diagonal blocks; blank: zeros."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _lib.structure import draw_structure
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.0))
draw_structure(axes[0], "benders", K=3, show_rhs=False)
axes[0].set_title("Benders: linking variables", fontsize=12)
draw_structure(axes[1], "dw", K=3, show_rhs=False)
axes[1].set_title("Dantzig–Wolfe: linking constraints", fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
